name: Bstrlib (The Better String Library)
baseline: C standard library char* string functions (string.h strcat/strcpy/strstr) for the C API; std::string for the CBString C++ wrapper
workload: Author's example benchmark programs (cbench.c for the C API against string.h, cppbench.cpp for CBString against std::string, mfcbench.cpp against MFC CString) timing char* assignment, character extraction, scan, concatenation and replace, run with five compiler/platform combinations.
claimed_speedup: Ratios on the page are Bstrlib/baseline in percent (legend '(bstring / Clib)' and '(CBString / std::string)'; above 100% means Bstrlib faster). C API vs C library, gcc 3.3.3 SUSE Linux column: concatenation 3980% (about 40x, derived from page data), assignment 91%, character extraction 113%, scan 89%, replace 86%; concatenation is 21700% (WATCOM), 23700% (VC++ 6.0), 21200% (Intel 6.0), 9260% (gcc Cygwin). CBString vs std::string, g++ 3.3.3 SUSE Linux column: concatenation 200%, scan 192%, replace 135%, assignment 132%, character extraction 100%; VC++ 6.0 concatenation 21100%, Intel 6.0 19400%, g++ Cygwin 1330%. Page also says default construction is far slower than std::string.
compiler_and_flags: Per column: WATCOM C/C++ 11.0c with STLport, Visual C++ 6.0 (12.00.8168), Intel C++ 6.0, GNU gcc/g++ 3.3.3 (Cygwin), GNU gcc/g++ 3.3.3 (SUSE Linux). Exact flags not stated; page says Bstrlib must be built at a maximum optimisation setting such as -O2 to match the already optimised standard library.
hardware: Athlon XP 1.620Ghz (first four columns: WATCOM, VC++ 6.0, Intel 6.0, g++ Cygwin) and Power 4 1Ghz (g++ SUSE Linux column), per the page's table header
tradeoffs: Length-tracked bstring header plus separately malloced buffer: extra allocation and per-string overhead for small strings; buffer grows to powers of two (up to about 2x(n+1) bytes) and never shrinks. Not a drop-in for char* or std::string (own API, bstring struct, CBString wrapper). Full bounds checking on CBString operator[] makes single-character extraction slower than unchecked STLs; CBString default constructor is non-trivial and slower than std::string's lazy one. Safety gain: avoids buffer overruns of the C string functions.
caveats: First-party numbers from the author's project page, run on 2004-era compilers (gcc 3.3.3, VC++ 6.0, Intel C++ 6.0, WATCOM 11.0c) and CPUs (Athlon XP, Power 4), so they say little about current libstdc++, libc++ or glibc. Compiler flags not stated; benchmark sources cbench.c, cppbench.cpp and mfcbench.cpp are named on the page but are not in the GitHub repo (raw fetch of cppbench.cpp and mfcbench.cpp returned 404), so the run is not reproducible from the repo. The enormous concatenation ratios compare repeated strcat (re-scans the destination every call) and Microsoft's O(m+n) STL concat against Bstrlib's length-tracked append, so they reflect idiom and an old STL, not general speed; the author notes the same for the STL case. On gcc (SUSE) the C API is slower than the C library for assignment (91%), scan (89%) and replace (86%), and CBString is slower than STLport for character extraction (63% WATCOM). Column for g++ SUSE ran on a different CPU than the others. bstrlib.txt also claims bsreadln can be 'several times faster' than fgets and Bstrlib 'dominates' C++ string benchmarks, with no numbers. Last commit 2016; the author calls it stable and well tested.

name: FreeGuard
baseline: DieHarder (secure allocator) and OpenBSD malloc; roughly parity with the default Linux (glibc) allocator
workload: Average program runtime overhead of each allocator relative to the default Linux allocator across the CCS 2017 paper's benchmark applications (application list not verified in this session).
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract, seen only in search-result snippets: average overhead below 2% relative to the default Linux allocator, versus secure allocators that can be up to 10x slower. A snippet describing the paper's evaluation gives OpenBSD malloc 22% and DieHarder over 36% average slowdown; later Guarder material from the same group quotes 31% and 74% instead, so these two figures are unconfirmed. Not a win over glibc: it is within about 2% of it.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.9.1 -O2 (from a search snippet of the paper's setup; DieHarder heap multiplier 8/7 and default settings; unverified)
hardware: 16-core Xeon E5-2640, Ubuntu 16.04 (from a search snippet of the paper's setup; unverified)
tradeoffs: Security-oriented drop-in malloc (LD_PRELOAD or link) guarding against heap overflow, use-after-free, double and invalid free; uses randomised, bag-based allocation, so memory overhead and Linux x86-64 only; make SSE2RNG=1 uses an SSE2 random number generator, plain make uses rand(). Dual licence: GPL-2.0 or a commercial licence purchased from UT San Antonio.
caveats: Snippet only: arxiv.org, ar5iv, usenix.net and patents.justia.com all returned getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND, so the paper's evaluation section was never opened and every number comes from WebSearch result summaries. The repo has no paper, benchmark scripts or results (6 commits, no benchmark directory); README only cites the CCS 2017 paper. A peer-reviewed paper would normally rate tier B; held at C because the numbers could not be read at the source, and the verifier should upgrade after reading the paper. The claim against glibc is parity (under 2% overhead), the speed win is only against other secure allocators (DieHarder, OpenBSD), and the DieHarder/OpenBSD percentages conflict between sources. Authors' own implementation. No commits since January 2018; the same group's successor is UTSASRG/Guarder.
